books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925

stimulus.text:
President Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925 (verbatim excerpt):

"After all, the chief business of the American people is business. They are profoundly concerned with producing, buying, selling, investing and prospering in the world. I am strongly of opinion that the great majority of people will always find these are moving impulses of our life."

"We make no concealment of the fact that we want wealth, but there are many other things that we want very much more. We want peace and honor, and that charity which is so strong an element of all civilization. The chief ideal of the American people is idealism."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpts from Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925, public domain (American Presidency Project).

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925
stem: The speech's claim that Americans want wealth but also “peace and honor” best supports which conclusion?

options.text: Coolidge limited his praise of business morally
Coolidge wanted newspapers to ignore all business
options.misconception: Coolidge spoke to newspaper editors about the press and business. He never asked the press to ignore business news.

options.text: Coolidge planned to tax wealth for schools
options.misconception: The speech says nothing about taxing wealth to fund schools. That plan is not in the passage.

options.text: Coolidge believed business would soon disappear
options.misconception: Coolidge expected business to keep growing. Nothing in the speech suggests business would disappear.

rationales.A: Coolidge praises business in one breath and sets moral limits on it in the next. The “peace and honor” line shows the praise was never without limits.
rationales.B: Coolidge spoke to newspaper editors about the press and business. He never asked the press to ignore business news.
rationales.C: The speech says nothing about taxing wealth to fund schools. That plan is not in the passage.
rationales.D: Coolidge expected business to keep growing. Nothing in the speech suggests business would disappear.
rationales.general:
1. Find the two claims: Americans want wealth, and they want peace and honor.
2. Ask what the second claim does: it puts a limit on the first.
3. Name the move: Coolidge praises business and still says it is not the whole of life.
Remember: when a speaker adds a limit to a bold claim, the limit is part of the argument.
